# Problem 1: Shared birthdays

I assume birthdays are independent and equally likely on each of
the 365 days of a non-leap year.

```{r birthday-function}
sim_birthday = function(n) {
  birthdays = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

set.seed(1)

sim_birthday(n = 23)
```

## Repeat the simulation

```{r birthday-simulation}
set.seed(1)

birthday_results =
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iteration = 1:10000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    shared_birthday = map_lgl(group_size, sim_birthday)
  )

birthday_summary =
  birthday_results |>
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarise(
    probability = mean(shared_birthday),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

birthday_summary |>
  filter(group_size %in% c(2, 10, 23, 30, 50)) |>
  knitr::kable(
    digits = 3,
    caption = "Estimated probability of at least one shared birthday"
  )
```

## Visualize the results

```{r birthday-plot}
birthday_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = probability)) +
  geom_line(color = "#287D8E", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#287D8E", size = 1.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(2, 10, 20, 30, 40, 50)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Probability of a shared birthday",
    x = "Number of people",
    y = "Estimated probability",
    caption = "10,000 simulations for each group size"
  )
```

For each group size, I estimated the probability of at least one shared
birthday as the proportion of 10,000 simulations that returned TRUE.
The estimated probability increases with group size: it is approximately
50% for 23 people and 97% for 50 people. Larger groups contain more possible
pairs of people, creating more opportunities for a shared birthday.

# Problem 2: Longitudinal study

## Import participant files

```{r study-import}
study_files =
  tibble(
    file_path = list.files(
      path = "data",
      pattern = "\\.csv$",
      recursive = TRUE,
      full.names = TRUE
    )
  ) |>
  mutate(
    file_name = basename(file_path)
  )

study_nested =
  study_files |>
  mutate(
    data = map(file_path, read_csv, show_col_types = FALSE)
  )

nrow(study_nested)

study_nested |>
  select(file_name, data)

study_nested$data[[1]]
```

## Tidy the data

```{r study-tidy}
study_df =
  study_nested |>
  select(file_name, data) |>
  mutate(
    subject_id = str_remove(file_name, "\\.csv$"),
    arm = recode(
      str_sub(subject_id, 1, 3),
      con = "Control",
      exp = "Experimental"
    )
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = data) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "outcome"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.integer(week)
  ) |>
  select(subject_id, arm, week, outcome) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

dim(study_df)

study_df |>
  head(8) |>
  knitr::kable(
    caption = "Weekly observations for the first participant"
  )
```

I combined the participant files using map() and unnest(), extracted
participant IDs and study arms from the filenames, and reshaped the
weekly measurements into long format. Participant IDs retain the arm
prefix to distinguish participants with the same number in different arms.

The tidy dataset contains 160 observations from 20 participants:
10 in the control arm and 10 in the experimental arm. Each participant
has measurements at eight weeks. Each row represents one participant
at one week, with columns for participant ID, study arm, week, and outcome.

## Plot individual trajectories

```{r study-spaghetti}
study_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = week,
      y = outcome,
      group = subject_id,
      color = arm
    )
  ) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7, linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5) +
  facet_grid(. ~ arm) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:8) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "Control" = "#287D8E",
      "Experimental" = "#E76F51"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly outcomes by study arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Outcome",
    caption = "Each line represents one participant"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

The control arm shows fluctuations over time without a clear overall
upward or downward trend. In contrast, participants in the experimental
arm generally show increasing outcomes over the eight weeks.
Both arms show differences between participants and week-to-week
variation within participants.

# Problem 3: Power of a one-sample t-test

## Simulation design

I simulated samples of 30 observations from normal distributions with
a population standard deviation of 5. The true means ranged from 0 to 6.
For each sample, I performed a two-sided one-sample t-test of a population
mean of zero, using a significance level of 0.05.

```{r t-test-function}
sim_t_test = function(mu, n = 30, sigma = 5) {
  sample_data = rnorm(
    n = n,
    mean = mu,
    sd = sigma
  )

  t.test(
    sample_data,
    mu = 0,
    alternative = "two.sided"
  ) |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(
      mu_hat = estimate,
      p_value = p.value
    )
}

set.seed(1)

sim_t_test(mu = 0)
```

## Repeat the simulation

```{r t-test-simulation}
set.seed(1)

test_results =
  expand_grid(
    true_mu = 0:6,
    iteration = 1:5000
  ) |>
  mutate(
    result = map(true_mu, sim_t_test)
  ) |>
  unnest(cols = result) |>
  mutate(
    reject = p_value < 0.05
  )

dim(test_results)

power_summary =
  test_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarise(
    n_sim = n(),
    n_reject = sum(reject),
    rejection_rate = mean(reject),
    mean_estimate = mean(mu_hat),
    mean_estimate_rejected = mean(mu_hat[reject]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  power_summary,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Simulation results by true population mean"
)
```

## Rejection rate and power

```{r power-plot}
power_summary |>
  ggplot(aes(x = true_mu, y = rejection_rate)) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0.05,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey55"
  ) +
  geom_line(color = "#287D8E", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(color = "#287D8E", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = scales::label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rejection rate of a one-sample t-test",
    subtitle = "n = 30; population SD = 5; 5,000 simulations per mean",
    x = "True population mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests rejected",
    caption = "Dashed line: 5% significance level"
  )
```

With sample size and population standard deviation fixed, power increases
as the true mean moves farther from the null value of zero.
The estimated power is 18.9% at a true mean of 1 and 88.7% at a true
mean of 3. At true means of 5 and 6, all 5,000 simulations reject the
null hypothesis, giving empirical rejection rates of 100%.

When the true mean is zero, the null hypothesis is true. The rejection
rate of approximately 5.1% therefore estimates the Type I error rate,
which is close to the chosen significance level of 5%.

## Compare mean estimates

```{r mean-estimate-plot}
estimate_plot_df =
  power_summary |>
  select(true_mu, mean_estimate, mean_estimate_rejected) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("mean_estimate"),
    names_to = "samples_used",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    samples_used = recode(
      samples_used,
      mean_estimate = "All samples",
      mean_estimate_rejected = "Rejected tests only"
    )
  )

estimate_plot_df |>
  ggplot(
    aes(
      x = true_mu,
      y = average_estimate,
      color = samples_used,
      shape = samples_used
    )
  ) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "grey55"
  ) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5) +
  scale_color_manual(
    values = c(
      "All samples" = "#287D8E",
      "Rejected tests only" = "#E76F51"
    )
  ) +
  scale_shape_manual(
    values = c(
      "All samples" = 16,
      "Rejected tests only" = 17
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Mean estimates across simulated samples",
    x = "True population mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = NULL,
    shape = NULL,
    caption = "Dashed line: average estimate equals the true mean"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Across all simulated samples, the average estimated mean is close to
the true mean, consistent with the sample mean being an unbiased estimator.

Restricting the analysis to rejected tests produces upward bias for small
positive true means. For example, when the true mean is 1, the average
estimate is approximately 0.996 across all samples but 2.214 among
rejected tests. Statistical significance depends on the estimated mean
relative to its standard error. With a small positive true effect,
rejected tests disproportionately include samples with upward fluctuations
in their estimated means.

As the true effect increases and power approaches one, most samples
are retained, so the two averages become similar. At a true mean of zero,
positive and negative significant estimates approximately balance in
this two-sided test, leaving their average close to zero.
